anti_patterns.approach: Blindly using history-based predictors for all jobs regardless of recurrence or temporal drift.
anti_patterns.why_it_tends_to_fail: History-based predictors assume recurrence and temporal stability; when jobs evolve (code, inputs, hardware), predictions become highly inaccurate (many jobs show >100% error), harming scheduling decisions.

anti_patterns.approach: Sampling an insufficient number of pilot tasks without checking intra-job task skew.
anti_patterns.why_it_tends_to_fail: If task-wise variance is large, too few samples produce unreliable estimates while still incurring scheduling delay, resulting in worse overall performance.

design_principles.statement: Learn job runtime properties in the spatial domain by sampling a small, representative set of tasks (pilot tasks) from each job before scheduling the remainder.
design_principles.why_it_matters: Provides accurate, online estimates for new or non-stationary jobs by exploiting per-job task homogeneity; avoids reliance on historical recurrence assumptions.

design_principles.statement: Decouple the predictor from the scheduler: let a modular predictor run pilot tasks to completion and feed learned estimates to a generic scheduler.
design_principles.why_it_matters: Modularity allows swapping or upgrading predictors without changing scheduling logic and isolates sampling overhead within the prediction component.

design_principles.statement: Choose prediction strategy based on measured variance: compare job-wise (temporal) variance vs task-wise (spatial) variance to decide between history-based and sampling-based learning.
design_principles.why_it_matters: Analytical relation between variances indicates which method yields better accuracy; enables adaptive selection of prediction approach and number of samples.

evidence.rationale: Paper describes SLearn: upon job arrival the predictor schedules sampled/pilot tasks to completion and uses observed task runtimes to estimate whole-job properties; this decouples prediction from scheduling.
evidence.statement: Task-sampling-based learning (SLearn) schedules a small set of pilot tasks of each job, observes their runtimes, and uses those observations to predict the job's runtime properties (learning in space).

evidence.rationale: Trace and Azure testbed results show median prediction errors and JCT improvements (examples: median errors 18.98%, 13.68%, 51.84% for SLearn vs 36.57%, 21.39%, 71.56% for 3Sigma; average JCT reductions of 1.28x, 1.56x, 1.32x).
evidence.statement: SLearn achieves substantially lower median prediction error and reduces average job completion time (JCT) versus a state-of-the-art history-based predictor across multiple production traces and testbed experiments.

evidence.rationale: Paper summarizes pros/cons along applicability, adaptiveness, accuracy, and runtime overhead, noting history-based has near-zero runtime cost while sampling incurs execution of pilot tasks and potential delay.
evidence.statement: Comparative properties: history-based (learning in time) is low-overhead and suitable for recurring/stable jobs; sampling-based (learning in space) applies to new jobs, adapts to change, may be more accurate depending on task skew, but incurs runtime overhead due to pilot tasks.

evidence.rationale: Analytical model shows prediction error depends on job-wise variance σ_o^2 and task-wise variance σ_1^2; sampling is favorable when σ_o^2 >> σ_1^2, and sampling accuracy improves as number of pilot tasks m increases.
evidence.statement: Analytical condition: sampling-based prediction outperforms history-based prediction when job-wise variation across time is large relative to task-wise variation (i.e., high inter-job variance and low intra-job task skew); sampling accuracy improves with more samples m.

evidence.rationale: Paper acknowledges the scheduling delay caused by pilot tasks and evaluates whether improved accuracy compensates; empirical results show improved JCT despite online overhead.
evidence.statement: Delaying scheduling of remaining tasks until pilot tasks finish introduces runtime overhead, but improved prediction accuracy from sampling can more than compensate and yield better overall job performance.

evidence.rationale: Paper cites literature and measurements showing many jobs are non-recurrent and that runtime properties evolve (code updates, machine heterogeneity), and cites 3Sigma's substantial prediction errors.
evidence.statement: History-based predictors fail when jobs are non-recurring or when runtime characteristics change due to software/hardware updates; e.g., 3Sigma produced >100% error for >23% of jobs in prior evaluation.

mechanisms.applicability: Distributed batch or data-parallel jobs composed of many similar tasks (e.g., map/reduce phases, Spark tasks); works for new and recurring jobs.
mechanisms.known_limits: Introduces runtime overhead because pilot tasks must run to completion before full scheduling; accuracy degrades if intra-job task skew is high (large task-wise variance); thin jobs with few tasks provide limited sampling opportunity.
mechanisms.name: SLearn (pilot-task sampling predictor)

mechanisms.applicability: Schedulers that optimize job-level metrics (e.g., average JCT) and can accept external per-job runtime estimates.
mechanisms.known_limits: Effectiveness depends on predictor accuracy; sampling-induced delays can reduce gains if not balanced by improved scheduling decisions.
mechanisms.name: Generic predictor-pluggable scheduler

title: A Case for Task Sampling based Learning for Cluster Job Scheduling

trade_offs.failure_modes: If task-wise variance is high or pilot sample size is too small, sampling yields poor estimates while incurring delay, worsening JCT; if sampling consumes scarce cluster capacity, it can increase queueing for other jobs.
trade_offs.objective_b: Runtime overhead / promptness of scheduling (delay before scheduling non-sampled tasks)
trade_offs.tension: Sampling pilot tasks increases online overhead and delays full job execution, but can reduce prediction error and enable better scheduling decisions that shorten overall JCT; benefit magnitude depends on task skew and number of samples.

trade_offs.failure_modes: Using history-based predictors on new or changed jobs yields large prediction errors; using sampling unnecessarily on stable, recurring jobs wastes resources.
trade_offs.tension: History-based approaches have near-zero runtime cost and are simple for recurring, stable jobs, whereas sampling-based approaches are applicable to new/non-stationary jobs but impose execution overhead.
